section: Prerequisites / why this matters
question: Why are FLOP counts alone not enough to predict how long a GPU kernel will take?
options: A kernel with few FLOPs can still be slow if it moves a lot of data across the memory hierarchy
FLOP counts ignore the time spent in the Python interpreter, which usually dominates GPU runtime
FLOP counts are only defined for matrix multiplies, so elementwise kernels have no FLOP count
GPUs execute FLOPs at a rate that varies randomly, so counts never correlate with runtime
explanation: Runtime depends on both arithmetic and data movement. A kernel that does very little arithmetic but drags a large tensor through HBM is limited by bandwidth, not by its FLOP count. This is why the memory hierarchy is needed alongside FLOP accounting to reason about performance.

section: Prerequisites / why this matters
question: What single governing fact about GPUs underlies most performance decisions for LLM kernels?
options: Arithmetic is expensive and moving data is cheap, so most LLM kernels are compute-bound
Kernel launches are free, so splitting work into many tiny kernels is always faster
Host RAM is faster than HBM, so tensors should be kept on the CPU whenever possible
Arithmetic is cheap and moving data is expensive, so most LLM kernels are memory-bound
explanation: A GPU can perform far more arithmetic per second than its memory can deliver bytes. As a result, most kernels outside the large matmuls spend their time waiting on data rather than computing. Recognizing this is what makes the roofline, fusion and FlashAttention make sense.

section: Prerequisites / why this matters
question: According to the GPU-performance view of training, how does FlashAttention achieve its speedup?
options: It approximates softmax with a cheaper polynomial, cutting the FLOPs per score
It skips attention for most token pairs, using a fixed block-sparse pattern
It avoids moving large intermediates through HBM, without reducing the math
It runs attention on the CPU while the GPU handles the projection matmuls
explanation: FlashAttention does essentially the same arithmetic as standard attention (slightly more, in fact). Its win comes from not writing and re-reading the large score matrices to and from HBM. Understanding where data lives explains why that is faster even though the math is not reduced.

section: 1. Intuition: a GPU is a very wide, very shallow factory
question: How does a typical CPU's design differ from a GPU's?
options: A CPU has thousands of simple lanes; a GPU has a few powerful out-of-order cores with big caches
A CPU has a few powerful out-of-order cores and big caches; a GPU has thousands of simple lanes
A CPU and a GPU share the same core design, but the GPU runs every core at a higher clock
A CPU has no caches, while a GPU relies on large branch predictors and out-of-order execution
explanation: A CPU is tuned to finish one complicated, branchy instruction stream as fast as possible, with 8–64 sophisticated cores. A GPU bets on raw parallel width: thousands of simple lanes executing the same operation across many data elements. The clock-speed answer is wrong because the difference is architectural, not frequency.

section: 1. Intuition: a GPU is a very wide, very shallow factory
question: What kind of workload is a CPU's design (deep out-of-order cores, branch prediction) best suited for?
options: Large dense matrix multiplications with no data dependency between output elements
Branchy, pointer-chasing code such as operating systems, web servers and compilers
Applying an activation function independently to every element of a huge tensor
Adding two vectors of a million floats element by element with no branches at all
explanation: Branch prediction and out-of-order execution help when the instruction stream is irregular and dependent, as in OS kernels, servers and compilers. Dense, uniform, branch-free work like matmuls and elementwise ops is the GPU's territory, because thousands of lanes can do it in parallel.

section: 1. Intuition: a GPU is a very wide, very shallow factory
question: Why does deep learning run 10–100x faster on GPUs than on CPUs?
options: It is mostly identical operations on many independent elements, run across thousands of lanes
Deep learning code is full of branches, which GPU branch predictors handle better than CPUs
GPUs have larger per-core caches than CPUs, so each individual operation finishes sooner
GPUs execute Python bytecode directly, avoiding the interpreter overhead that CPUs suffer
explanation: Matmuls, vector adds and elementwise activations have no branching and no dependency between elements, so the same instruction can be applied across thousands of lanes at once. That data-parallel structure maps directly onto GPU hardware. GPUs are not better at branches; branchy code is actually expensive on them.

section: 1. Intuition: a GPU is a very wide, very shallow factory
question: What is usually the real performance question on a GPU?
options: Whether there are enough arithmetic units to perform the required FLOPs
Whether the CPU clock speed is high enough to run the kernels
Whether the kernel's code has been compiled with optimization flags
Whether data can be delivered to the compute units fast enough
explanation: GPU arithmetic units can consume numbers much faster than memory can supply them. So the bottleneck is rarely raw compute; it is almost always feeding data to the lanes. This is the theme of the whole GPU-performance module.

section: 1. Intuition: a GPU is a very wide, very shallow factory
question: Because a GPU trades single-thread cleverness for raw parallel width, which resource becomes scarce?
options: Arithmetic throughput
Instruction decoding
Data movement
Branch prediction capacity
explanation: With thousands of lanes, arithmetic is abundant and cheap. The scarce resource is moving data to those lanes, so most GPU optimization is about not moving data you do not have to. Arithmetic throughput is the abundant resource, not the scarce one.

section: 2. The execution hierarchy: threads, warps, blocks, SMs
question: In NVIDIA's CUDA execution model, what is a thread?
options: A group of 32 lanes that execute the same instruction in lockstep on different data
The physical processor that holds a register file, shared memory and Tensor Cores
The smallest unit of work: one lane running the kernel, usually on one element
A group of warps guaranteed to run on the same SM and share its on-chip memory
explanation: A thread is the finest unit: one lane running the kernel on (usually) one element, and a launch can create millions of them. A group of 32 lockstep threads is a warp, a group of warps on one SM is a thread block, and the physical processor is the SM.

section: 2. The execution hierarchy: threads, warps, blocks, SMs
question: How many threads make up a warp on NVIDIA GPUs?
explanation: Threads execute in lockstep groups of 32 called warps. 1024 is the maximum size of a thread block, not a warp. The warp is the real unit of scheduling: the hardware issues one instruction per warp.

section: 2. The execution hierarchy: threads, warps, blocks, SMs
question: What does SIMT (single instruction, multiple threads) mean for the threads of a warp?
options: All threads in the warp execute the same instruction at the same time, each on its own data
Each thread in the warp runs a different instruction stream independently
Only one thread in the warp runs at a time while the others wait
The threads of a warp share a single register so they always compute the same value
explanation: In SIMT, the 32 threads of a warp are issued one instruction together, and each applies it to its own data element. The hardware issues instructions per warp, not per thread. Threads are not independent instruction streams, which is why divergence costs performance.

section: 2. The execution hierarchy: threads, warps, blocks, SMs
question: What is the real unit of scheduling on an NVIDIA GPU?
options: The individual thread: each thread is scheduled independently
The whole kernel: the GPU schedules one kernel instruction at a time across all SMs
The SM: one instruction is issued per SM for all its threads
The warp: the hardware issues one instruction per warp
explanation: Although threads are the smallest unit of work, the hardware issues instructions to whole warps of 32 threads. That is why warp-level behaviour (lockstep execution, divergence, latency hiding by switching warps) matters for performance.

section: 2. The execution hierarchy: threads, warps, blocks, SMs
question: What property distinguishes a thread block (CTA) from an arbitrary set of threads?
options: Its threads are guaranteed to be spread across different SMs for load balancing
Its threads each get a private region of HBM that no other block is allowed to read
It always contains exactly 32 threads that execute the same instruction in lockstep
Its warps share one SM, so they can use shared memory and sync at a barrier
explanation: A thread block is a group of warps (up to 1024 threads) placed together on one SM. That placement lets them share a fast scratchpad (shared memory) and synchronize with a barrier. Exactly 32 lockstep threads describes a warp, not a block.

section: 2. The execution hierarchy: threads, warps, blocks, SMs
question: What is the maximum number of threads in a single CUDA thread block?
explanation: A thread block can hold up to 1024 threads, organized as warps of 32. 32 is the warp size and 108 is the number of SMs on an A100.

section: 2. The execution hierarchy: threads, warps, blocks, SMs
question: Which capability of thread blocks does FlashAttention exploit?
options: A block can write directly into another GPU's HBM without going through NVLink
A block can load a tile into shared memory once and have all its threads reuse it
A block can skip computing scores whose values its threads predict to be small
A block can be spread over several SMs at once to get access to more registers
explanation: Threads in a block share on-chip shared memory and can synchronize. FlashAttention uses this to stage tiles of Q, K and V in shared memory once and reuse them across many computations, instead of repeatedly reading from HBM. A block is never split across SMs.

section: 2. The execution hierarchy: threads, warps, blocks, SMs
question: How many streaming multiprocessors (SMs) do an A100 and an H100 have, respectively?
options: 32 and 64
explanation: An A100 has 108 SMs and an H100 has 132. The numbers 80 and 141 are HBM capacities in GB, and 1024 is the maximum thread-block size.

section: 2. The execution hierarchy: threads, warps, blocks, SMs
question: What are Tensor Cores?
options: Dedicated matrix-multiply-accumulate units in each SM that do most transformer FLOPs
A separate chip next to the GPU that stores tensors between consecutive kernel launches
The portion of HBM reserved for model weights so they are never evicted during training
Software threads PyTorch uses to schedule tensor operations from the CPU onto the GPU
explanation: Each SM contains, along with its register file, shared memory and warp schedulers, a set of arithmetic units including Tensor Cores. These are specialized matrix-multiply-accumulate units, and they perform most of the FLOPs in transformer training. They are hardware compute units, not memory.

section: 2. The execution hierarchy: threads, warps, blocks, SMs
question: In GPU terminology, what is a kernel?
options: A single SM together with its private register file and its shared memory
The operating-system driver that copies tensors from host RAM into the HBM
A group of 32 threads that execute the same instruction in lockstep on an SM
One function launched across a whole grid of threads, blocks and SMs
explanation: A kernel is one GPU function, launched over a grid of many thread blocks that the GPU distributes across its SMs. The hierarchy is thread, warp, thread block, SM, GPU. A group of 32 lockstep threads is a warp.

section: Two consequences worth remembering
question: Why do GPUs want many warps in flight (high occupancy)?
options: Because each additional resident warp raises the clock speed of the SM it runs on
Because warps share registers, so more warps means more registers for every thread
So a warp stalled on memory can be swapped for a ready one, keeping units busy
Because a kernel can only start once every SM is filled with exactly one warp of work
explanation: Many warps are about latency hiding, not per-warp speed. When a warp waits on a slow memory read, the SM switches instantly to another ready warp so the units never sit idle. More warps actually means fewer registers per thread, since the register file is shared.

section: Two consequences worth remembering
question: Why can a training run with a tiny batch or very short sequence show low MFU even though the kernels are correct?
options: Tiny batches force every operation to run in fp64, which is much slower on Tensor Cores
Too few warps exist to hide memory latency, so arithmetic units idle during stalls
Short sequences make attention compute-bound, which leaves the Tensor Cores starved
The GPU disables its Tensor Cores whenever the batch size falls below 32 sequences
explanation: With too little parallel work, the scheduler has no other ready warp to switch to when one stalls on memory. The arithmetic units then idle, and model FLOPs utilization drops. This is one concrete cause of very low MFU numbers on small workloads.

section: Two consequences worth remembering
question: What happens when the threads of one warp take different sides of an if statement?
options: Each thread runs only its own path in parallel with the others, at no extra cost
The warp runs both paths in turn, masking inactive threads, which wastes throughput
The GPU moves the diverging threads to a different SM so each path runs separately
The kernel aborts with a launch error, because divergent branches are not allowed
explanation: Because a warp issues one instruction for all 32 threads, divergent threads cannot run their paths simultaneously. The warp runs both paths in turn and masks out threads not on the current path. Data-parallel numeric code avoids this, which is part of why deep learning suits GPUs.

section: 3. The memory hierarchy: the central object of this module
question: What trade-off defines the levels of the GPU memory hierarchy?
options: Size against speed: small memories are fast and near the units, large ones slow and far
Precision against range: each lower level stores numbers in a lower-precision format
Cost against reliability: the larger, cheaper levels lose or corrupt data more often
Read speed against write speed: each level is fast for one but slow for the other
explanation: The hierarchy trades capacity for speed. Each level down is roughly 10x bigger and several times slower. Registers are tiny and instant; host RAM is huge and slowest.

section: 3. The memory hierarchy: the central object of this module
question: Which ordering of GPU memory levels runs from fastest/smallest to slowest/largest?
options: Shared memory/SRAM, registers, HBM, L2 cache, host RAM
Registers, L2 cache, shared memory/SRAM, host RAM, HBM
HBM, L2 cache, shared memory/SRAM, registers, host RAM
Registers, shared memory/SRAM, L2 cache, HBM, host RAM
explanation: The order is registers (per-thread, instant), shared memory/SRAM (per-SM scratchpad), L2 (one cache for the whole GPU), HBM (the large off-chip 'GPU memory') and host RAM (CPU memory across PCIe). Each step down is bigger and slower.

section: 3. The memory hierarchy: the central object of this module
question: Why does each GPU thread get only a few dozen registers?
options: Registers are stored in HBM, which limits how many each thread can address
Each thread is allowed exactly one register for every warp it belongs to
An SM's ~256 KB register file is split across all of its live threads
Registers are pooled across all SMs, so each thread gets a slice of the whole GPU
explanation: Registers are per-thread private storage physically inside the SM, with effectively zero-cycle access. But the whole SM has a register file of roughly 256 KB, divided among all live threads, so each thread has only a few dozen registers. Registers are on-chip, not in HBM.

section: 3. The memory hierarchy: the central object of this module
question: Roughly how much shared memory (SRAM) is available per SM on an A100 and an H100?
options: About 40 MB on A100 and about 50 MB on H100
About 80 GB on A100 and about 141 GB on H100
Up to about 164 KB on A100 and about 228 KB on H100
About 256 bytes on A100 and about 512 bytes on H100
explanation: Shared memory is a small configurable scratchpad per SM: up to ~164 KB on A100 and ~228 KB on H100. The 40–50 MB figures are the L2 cache for the whole GPU, and 80–141 GB are HBM capacities.

section: 3. The memory hierarchy: the central object of this module
question: Why is the aggregate bandwidth of on-chip shared memory enormous even though each SM's scratchpad is small?
options: Shared memory is one cache spanning all SMs, connected by a single 1 PB/s bus
Each SM gets a few hundred GB/s and there are 100+ SMs, so tens of TB/s in total
Shared memory is backed by HBM, so it simply inherits HBM's multi-TB/s bandwidth
Shared memory compresses tiles on the fly, so each access moves far fewer bytes
explanation: Shared memory is per-SM and on-chip, with a few hundred GB/s per SM. Multiplied across ~100+ SMs, aggregate on-chip bandwidth reaches tens of TB/s, far above HBM's ~2–3 TB/s. That is why staging data in SRAM pays off.

section: 3. The memory hierarchy: the central object of this module
question: Which memory level does FlashAttention use to stage tiles of Q, K and V so it can do lots of arithmetic without going back to HBM?
options: Shared memory / SRAM
The GPU-wide L2 cache
Pinned host RAM
HBM, the off-chip DRAM
explanation: FlashAttention lives in shared memory: it loads tiles of Q, K and V into the per-SM SRAM and does many operations on them there. The point is to avoid HBM traffic, so HBM is the level it minimizes, not the one it stages in.

section: 3. The memory hierarchy: the central object of this module
question: What is the L2 cache on an A100/H100-class GPU?
options: A private per-thread store of a few dozen values with effectively instant access
A per-SM scratchpad of up to ~228 KB that each thread block manages explicitly
The off-chip DRAM stack of 40–80 GB holding weights, gradients and activations
One ~40–50 MB cache shared by all SMs that caches recent HBM data automatically
explanation: L2 is one cache for the whole GPU (~40 MB A100, ~50 MB H100). It caches recent HBM accesses automatically and sits between SRAM and HBM in speed. The explicitly managed per-SM scratchpad is shared memory, and the off-chip DRAM is HBM.

section: 3. The memory hierarchy: the central object of this module
question: When someone says 'an 80 GB A100', which memory level are they referring to?
options: The L2 cache shared by all SMs on the die
The total shared memory of all SMs combined
The host RAM the GPU reaches over PCIe
HBM, the off-chip DRAM stacked by the die
explanation: The quoted 'GPU memory' is HBM (High-Bandwidth Memory), off-chip DRAM stacked beside the die. It is where weights, gradients, optimizer state and activations live. L2 and shared memory are tiny by comparison.

section: 3. The memory hierarchy: the central object of this module
question: Roughly what HBM bandwidth do the A100 and H100 provide?
options: About 32–64 GB/s on both, set by the PCIe link
About 312 TB/s on A100 and 990 TB/s on H100
About 1.5–2 TB/s on A100 and 3.3 TB/s on H100
About tens of TB/s on both, like on-chip SRAM
explanation: HBM bandwidth is ~1.5–2 TB/s on A100 and ~3.3 TB/s on H100. 32–64 GB/s is PCIe to host RAM, and tens of TB/s is aggregate on-chip SRAM bandwidth. 312 is the A100's bf16 TFLOP/s figure, not a bandwidth.

section: 3. The memory hierarchy: the central object of this module
question: Where do a model's weights, gradients, optimizer state and activations actually live during GPU training?
options: In the L2 cache
In HBM
In registers
In shared memory
explanation: These large tensors live in HBM, the big off-chip GPU memory. Every time a kernel reads a tensor 'from GPU memory', it reads from HBM. Registers, shared memory and L2 are far too small to hold them.

section: 3. The memory hierarchy: the central object of this module
question: Why should tensors be moved from host to device (or between GPUs) rarely?
options: PCIe/NVLink is about 10x slower than HBM, so every crossing is a bottleneck
Each transfer permanently reduces the HBM capacity available to the program
Host-to-device copies silently upcast the tensor's dtype to fp64 on arrival
The GPU must flush and reset its L2 cache and all SMs after every transfer
explanation: Host RAM is reached over PCIe (~32–64 GB/s) or NVLink, an order of magnitude slower than HBM. Calling .to('cuda') or moving data between GPUs crosses this slow link, so the practice is to move data to the GPU once and keep it there.

section: Representative numbers (approximate — orders of magnitude, not spec sheets)
question: Relative to HBM bandwidth, roughly how fast is host RAM accessed over PCIe?
options: About 0.02–0.03x of HBM
About 2–5x faster than HBM
About 10–20x faster than HBM
About the same speed as HBM
explanation: PCIe gives ~32–64 GB/s against HBM's ~1.5–3.3 TB/s, about 0.02–0.03x. The 2–5x figure is L2 and 10–20x is shared memory, both faster than HBM.

section: Representative numbers (approximate — orders of magnitude, not spec sheets)
question: Why should the GPU memory sizes and bandwidths quoted for A100/H100 be treated as orders of magnitude rather than exact specs?
options: Bandwidth figures drift every time the GPU is rebooted, so no value is stable for long
Vendors publish no official figures, so every quoted number is a community estimate
The effective values depend on the Python and PyTorch versions used to run the model
They vary by SKU (40 vs 80 GB, SXM vs PCIe) and by peak vs sustained quoting
explanation: The numbers are ballpark, publicly documented figures. Real values differ between variants such as 40 GB vs 80 GB A100 or SXM vs PCIe, and between peak and sustained quotes. They are meant for reasoning, not for spec-sheet precision.

section: Representative numbers (approximate — orders of magnitude, not spec sheets)
question: Which two A100 numbers should be held side by side to understand GPU performance?
options: About 108 SMs and about 32 threads per warp
About 40 MB of L2 and 256 KB of registers per SM
About 2 TB/s HBM and about 312 TFLOP/s bf16
About 80 GB of HBM and about 64 GB/s of PCIe
explanation: Comparing ~312 TFLOP/s of bf16 compute with ~2 TB/s of HBM bandwidth reveals how many FLOPs the chip can do per byte read. That ratio is what decides whether a kernel is memory-bound or compute-bound.

section: 4. The central fact: arithmetic is cheap, data movement is expensive
question: Roughly how many FLOPs can an A100 perform in the time it reads one byte from HBM?
options: About 1
About 150
About 15
About 1500
explanation: Dividing ~312x10^12 FLOP/s by ~2x10^12 bytes/s gives about 156 FLOPs per byte. A kernel needs at least that many FLOPs per byte of HBM traffic to keep the arithmetic units busy.

section: 4. The central fact: arithmetic is cheap, data movement is expensive
question: A kernel reads a byte from HBM and does only one or two FLOPs with it before needing the next byte. On an A100, what happens?
options: The kernel is compute-bound, because each FLOP has to wait for the FLOP before it
The arithmetic units idle ~99% of the time waiting on data: it is memory-bound
The kernel runs at peak FLOP/s, because it does so little work for each byte read
The kernel automatically keeps its data in registers, so HBM is never read again
explanation: The A100 can do ~150 FLOPs per HBM byte. Doing only 1–2 FLOPs per byte leaves the units waiting almost all the time, so runtime is set by how fast HBM delivers bytes. That is the definition of a memory-bound (bandwidth-bound) kernel.

section: 4. The central fact: arithmetic is cheap, data movement is expensive
question: What makes a kernel compute-bound?
options: It does hundreds of FLOPs per byte loaded, like a large matmul reusing each value
It reads very large tensors from HBM and does one FLOP per element it loads
It launches thousands of tiny kernels in a row, each saturating the Tensor Cores
It moves data between the CPU and GPU every step, keeping the PCIe link busy
explanation: A compute-bound kernel has enough arithmetic per byte that the arithmetic units stay saturated and memory is not the bottleneck. Large matmuls achieve this by reusing each loaded value across a whole row or column of outputs. Elementwise ops over big tensors are the classic memory-bound case.

section: 4. The central fact: arithmetic is cheap, data movement is expensive
question: Which of these transformer operations is typically memory-bound on a GPU?
options: The QKV projection matmul
The MLP up-projection matmul
The attention output projection matmul
LayerNorm
explanation: Elementwise and reduction operations such as activations, LayerNorm, dropout, bias add, softmax and the attention score matrix are memory-bound. The large weight matmuls (QKV, output projection, MLP layers) reuse each loaded value many times and are compute-bound.

section: Why LLM kernels are so often memory-bound
question: Why are the big weight matmuls in a transformer (QKV, output projection, MLP) considered 'good' from a performance standpoint?
options: They are memory-bound, which makes them the easiest ops to speed up with fusion
They do almost no FLOPs, so they finish instantly compared with elementwise ops
They are compute-bound: each loaded number is reused, keeping Tensor Cores busy
They run on the CPU in parallel, freeing the GPU for the attention computation
explanation: These matmuls are the 6N FLOPs of training and genuinely compute-bound. Each loaded value participates in many multiply-adds, so the Tensor Cores stay saturated. The inefficiency lies in the elementwise and reduction ops around them.

section: Why LLM kernels are so often memory-bound
question: Why can the many small elementwise and reduction ops between transformer matmuls eat a large share of wall-clock time despite having few FLOPs?
options: Each one is dispatched to the CPU instead of the GPU, adding a PCIe round trip
Each one recomputes the whole forward pass from scratch to get its inputs back
Each reads a big activation from HBM and writes it back, a bandwidth-bound trip
Each one forces the GPU into fp64 precision, which runs at a fraction of peak
explanation: Ops like bias add, GELU, dropout, LayerNorm, residual add and softmax do tiny arithmetic per element but read and write whole activation tensors in HBM. Their arithmetic intensity is near the floor, so their runtime is set by bandwidth, and summed together they cost a lot.

section: Why LLM kernels are so often memory-bound
question: Which attention-related cost is singled out as a crucial memory-bound part of the transformer forward pass?
options: Loading the Q, K and V weight matrices, which are kept in fp32
The softmax and the reading/writing of the T x T score matrix
The positional embedding lookup repeated at every layer
The token embedding matmul over the whole vocabulary
explanation: Among the memory-bound tail, the attention softmax and the T x T score matrix traffic stand out, since that matrix grows quadratically with sequence length. FlashAttention is designed specifically to stop touching HBM for it.

section: Why LLM kernels are so often memory-bound
question: Which pairing correctly matches the next GPU-performance tools to the memory-bound problem?
options: Roofline/fusion: measure and cut round trips; profiler/mixed precision: find kernels, halve bytes; FlashAttention: skip HBM
Roofline/fusion: halve bytes and add FLOPs; profiler/mixed precision: fuse kernels; FlashAttention: raise score precision
Roofline/mixed precision: find hot kernels; fusion: halve bytes per element; FlashAttention: move scores to host RAM
Profiler/fusion: change dtypes; roofline: avoid HBM entirely; FlashAttention: time kernels and approximate the softmax
explanation: The roofline quantifies memory-bound versus compute-bound and fusion cuts HBM round trips. The profiler finds the offending kernels and mixed precision halves the bytes moved. FlashAttention rebuilds attention so the score matrix never goes to HBM.

section: 5. Tensor shapes, dtype, device — where a tensor physically lives
question: What does a PyTorch tensor's device attribute tell you physically on a GPU system?
options: How many bytes each element occupies, such as 4 for fp32
How many elements the tensor holds across all its dimensions
Which SM will execute the next operation on the tensor
Which memory holds the bytes: host RAM, or GPU N's HBM
explanation: device says where the bytes are stored: 'cpu' means host RAM and 'cuda:0' means the HBM of GPU 0. Bytes per element is the dtype, and element count comes from the shape.

section: 5. Tensor shapes, dtype, device — where a tensor physically lives
question: What physically happens when you call x.to('cuda') on a CPU tensor?
options: The tensor is marked as GPU-ready but stays in host RAM until first use, at no cost
The tensor is moved into the L2 cache of every SM
The tensor's dtype is converted to bf16 for the GPU
The tensor's bytes are copied across the PCIe bus into the GPU's HBM
explanation: x.to('cuda') performs a real copy across the slow PCIe link into HBM. Because that transfer is slow, data should be moved to the GPU once and kept there. It does not change the dtype.

section: 5. Tensor shapes, dtype, device — where a tensor physically lives
question: How does a tensor's dtype affect GPU performance?
options: It only affects numerical accuracy and has no effect on the bytes each op must move
It decides which SM the tensor is stored on, and so which SM runs ops that use it
It sets bytes per element, so it fixes both HBM storage and bytes moved per op
It sets the number of elements in the tensor, and so how many threads are launched
explanation: dtype fixes the element size: fp32 is 4 bytes and bf16/fp16 are 2 bytes. That size multiplies both storage and the bandwidth cost of every op reading or writing the tensor, so halving it halves both — the core performance argument for mixed precision.

section: 5. Tensor shapes, dtype, device — where a tensor physically lives
question: How is the total byte size of a PyTorch tensor computed?
options: numel() divided by element_size()
numel() times element_size()
The product of the shape dimensions only, ignoring dtype
element_size() times the number of dimensions
explanation: The total bytes are the number of elements (from the shape) times bytes per element (from the dtype). The shape alone gives element count but not bytes.

section: 5. Tensor shapes, dtype, device — where a tensor physically lives
question: Why did the GPT-2-small logits tensor of shape (8, 1024, 50257) in fp32 dominate the activation memory bucket?
options: It is about 1.65 GB, written to HBM by the final matmul and read back by the loss
It is kept in host RAM and must cross the PCIe bus twice in every training step
It is stored in fp64 by default, which doubles its size relative to the hidden states
It is recomputed from scratch in every layer, so its traffic is multiplied by n_layer
explanation: 8 x 1024 x 50257 x 4 bytes is about 1.65 GB. That much data is written to HBM and read back by the loss, so its size directly sets its HBM cost and memory footprint. Its large vocabulary dimension is what makes it so big.

section: 5. Tensor shapes, dtype, device — where a tensor physically lives
question: What does F.gelu(x) do on the GPU for an activation x of shape (B, T, 4C) in HBM?
options: A kernel reads every element of x from HBM, does a few FLOPs each, and writes y back
GELU runs entirely inside the L2 cache, so x and y never need to touch HBM at all
PyTorch sends x to the CPU, applies GELU there with SIMD, and copies the result back
GELU runs on the Tensor Cores as a matrix multiply against a precomputed lookup table
explanation: The GELU kernel reads x from HBM, computes a handful of FLOPs per element in registers, and writes y back. Bytes moved are a full read plus a full write, with tiny arithmetic, making it a textbook memory-bound kernel and a prime fusion candidate.

section: 6. Under the hood: what happens when you call one PyTorch op on the GPU
question: When PyTorch runs c = a + b on CUDA tensors, what is the first thing that happens?
options: The GPU immediately starts reading a and b from HBM without the CPU being involved
PyTorch copies a and b back to host RAM so it can check their shapes and dtypes
The SMs JIT-compile a new kernel from the Python source of the expression a + b
PyTorch's C++ dispatcher selects the CUDA kernel for that op and dtype
explanation: The Python call goes into PyTorch's C++ dispatcher, which picks the right kernel (here elementwise add for fp16 on CUDA). Then PyTorch launches that kernel, which the GPU schedules across its SMs.

section: 6. Under the hood: what happens when you call one PyTorch op on the GPU
question: Why is launching thousands of tiny GPU kernels slow?
options: Each launch reloads the model weights from host RAM before the kernel can start
Each launch forces the GPU to clear and re-zero the HBM regions it will write
Each launch has a fixed overhead of a few microseconds, however little work it does
Each launch can only use a single SM, so thousands of kernels serialize on one SM
explanation: Every kernel launch costs a few microseconds of fixed overhead. With thousands of tiny kernels this overhead adds up, which is one reason fusing ops into fewer kernels helps.

section: 6. Under the hood: what happens when you call one PyTorch op on the GPU
question: In c = a + b for fp16 tensors of shape (4096, 4096), what is the approximate arithmetic intensity and what does it imply?
options: About 170 FLOPs/byte, above the ~150 ridge, so the kernel is compute-bound
About 0.17 FLOPs/byte, far below the ~150 ridge, so the kernel is memory-bound
About 1.7 FLOPs/byte, just at the ridge for fp16, so the kernel is balanced
About 150 FLOPs/byte, right at the ridge, so it runs near peak FLOP/s
explanation: The add does one FLOP per element (~1.7x10^7 FLOPs) while moving two reads and one write of 2-byte elements (~100 MB). That gives ~0.17 FLOPs/byte, hopelessly below the ~150 ridge, so runtime is set by HBM bandwidth.

section: 6. Under the hood: what happens when you call one PyTorch op on the GPU
question: For an elementwise add that moves about 100 MB on an A100, what sets its runtime?
options: Peak FLOP/s: about 1.7x10^7 FLOPs / 312 TFLOP/s, well under a microsecond
HBM bandwidth: about 100 MB / 2 TB/s ≈ 50 µs, with the math hidden behind it
Kernel launch overhead alone, since one launch dwarfs any data the add moves
PCIe bandwidth: about 100 MB / 64 GB/s, since the inputs come from host RAM
explanation: Because the kernel is memory-bound, its runtime is essentially bytes moved divided by HBM bandwidth, about 50 microseconds. The arithmetic is essentially free and overlaps with the memory traffic. PCIe is not involved since the tensors are already in HBM.

section: Check yourself
question: Why does a GPU want thousands of threads in flight even though it can physically execute only a limited number at once?
options: Extra warps hide memory latency: the scheduler runs others while some wait on HBM
More resident threads raise the clock speed of each SM through dynamic boosting
Each extra thread brings its own share of HBM bandwidth, so total bandwidth grows
The GPU driver rejects any kernel launched with fewer than a thousand threads
explanation: The extra threads are latency hiding, not raw throughput. When a warp stalls on a slow HBM read, the SM switches to another ready warp. With too few warps, the units idle during every stall and utilization collapses.

section: Check yourself
question: A GELU over a (B, T, 4C) activation does few FLOPs per element. What is the fix for its cost, as previewed for the roofline/fusion discussion?
options: Rewrite GELU with a cheaper approximation so it does fewer FLOPs per element
Run GELU on the CPU in parallel so the GPU is free for the next matmul
Assign more SMs to the GELU kernel so its arithmetic finishes sooner
Fuse GELU with the bias add and dropout so intermediates stay on chip
explanation: GELU is memory-bound: its cost is the HBM round trip of a big tensor, not its arithmetic. Fusing it with bias add and dropout means one HBM read and one write instead of three round trips. Reducing FLOPs would barely help since arithmetic is not the bottleneck.
